messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 55‑year‑old Ghanaian‑born painter who has lived in the United States for nearly thirty years. He is married to Adwoa, and they have two grown children. Eighteen months ago his younger brother Kwame was killed in a hit‑and‑run accident. Kofi received the news by phone while he was painting the exterior of a suburban home. He drove to the hospital but his brother was already dead; the only image that stuck was the blank sheet covering Kwame’s body and the sound of a siren fading outside the emergency bay. 

In the weeks that followed, Kofi began to notice changes he could not explain. He would be standing on a scaffold, brush in hand, when the wail of a distant ambulance would send a jolt through his chest. His body would lock tight—shoulders hunched, jaw clenched—and he would scan the street for danger, even though the siren was blocks away. At first he told himself it was just grief, but the vigilance did not fade. At home, after dark, he found himself unable to settle. He would check the locks twice, then sit on the edge of the bed, listening. Adwoa would ask what he was listening for, and he could not answer. He only knew that the night felt unsafe, that his body was constantly coiled, ready to react. He felt on guard even inside his own bedroom.

The memories came in two forms. Sometimes a clear image would surface—Kwame’s face, or the hospital corridor—and Kofi would be flooded with a grief so physical it felt like a weight on his chest. Other times the grief arrived without any image at all, a sudden overwhelming sadness that seemed to come from nowhere, leaving him disoriented and shaken.  

Work became a minefield. Every job site became a potential reminder of the phone call he had taken on that other job site. When a client mentioned losing a parent in passing, Kofi felt his throat close. He started turning down residential jobs that required him to work near busy roads, though he did not say why to his boss. He began to believe that his life had been destroyed by the accident. He no longer recognised himself. He had always been a steady, easy‑going man; now he was tense, withdrawn, and easily startled. He felt isolated and set apart from everyone, even from Adwoa, who tried to comfort him but could not understand why he would flinch when she touched his shoulder at night.  

The more isolated he felt, the more he saw the world through a lens of danger. A car backfiring in the street, a neighbour’s raised voice, the smell of antiseptic in a pharmacy—each seemed to confirm that something terrible was about to happen. The constant tension made him hypersensitive to any reminder of Kwame’s death. If he heard the word “brother” in conversation, his stomach dropped. He began to avoid social gatherings where people might ask about his family.  

The memories themselves fed the cycle. A sudden visual image of Kwame laughing would hit him while he was driving, and he would grip the steering wheel so hard his knuckles turned white, his heart racing, his eyes darting to the rear‑view mirror as if he were being followed. That rush of fear made him anticipate triggers everywhere. He started leaving work early, claiming headaches. He would lie in bed at night, body rigid, replaying the moment of the phone call even though he had no clear image of it—only the emotion, raw and crushing.  

By the time he sought help at his wife’s insistence, Kofi was barely functioning. He had lost two contracts and was avoiding most of his usual painting routes. He was sleeping three hours a night, if that. What frightened him most was the feeling that the man he used to be—competent, connected, at ease in his own skin—had disappeared completely. He wanted to believe that could change, but the sirens seemed to be waiting everywhere, and he did not know how to stop listening for them.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals (e.g., belief life destroyed) cause or influence intrusive memories.
The vignette lacks a causal link where negative appraisals lead to increased perception or occurrence of triggers.
The vignette does not convey that intrusive memories directly lead to or reinforce negative appraisals such as feeling destroyed or isolated.
The vignette does not establish that memories themselves cause triggers; the connection is only indirect via threat.
